chapters.question_prompt: After construction, ground rent, vacancy and upkeep, what does a highway billboard actually earn?
chapters.title: Billboard Unit Economics: The Full Accounting
chapters.subtitle: Structure costs vs. permit value, ground rent during vacancy, occupancy and rate math, Lamar's revenue concentration, and building a billboard empire
chapters.executive_summary: Sixteen operators and analysts agree on one thesis: the permit is the asset, not the steel, and occupancy decides whether it pays. The 1965 Highway Beautification Act, local moratoriums, and four state bans freeze supply, so buying an existing permitted structure beats building a new one. Ground rent takes 15 to 25% of revenue. Static boards clear thin margins that leverage can erase. Operators underwrite at 85% occupancy rather than at rate card. Digital conversion turns a static face earning roughly $3,000 a month into $15,000 to $18,000 a month for about $200,000, and ledgerandland models net income nearly tripling. The practitioners split on entry cost, on exit multiples (3-5x versus 7-12x revenue), and on market size ($9.46B versus $57.8B). They also split on how much debt a board can carry before the mortgage crushes a money-making asset.

key_metrics.label: Digital Conversion Revenue Uplift
key_metrics.value: $3,000/mo static to $15,000-$18,000/mo digital for ~$200,000
key_metrics.context: Lamar CEO Sean Reilly's numbers for converting a static face to digital. Analysts put the return at roughly 43% after a 20% lease and a 7% commission.

key_metrics.label: Occupancy Underwriting Threshold
key_metrics.value: 85% occupancy (about 44 sold weeks per year)
key_metrics.context: The operator heuristic for billboard investment, used to underwrite acquisitions against realistic fill instead of a full calendar.

key_metrics.label: Static Board Breakeven Fill
key_metrics.value: ~38% fill to break even; ~$800 loss at 35% fill
key_metrics.context: Model of a $40,000 build selling $2,000 per four-week block across 13 blocks, with $9,000 fixed costs plus 10% variable costs.

key_metrics.label: Exit Valuation Multiple
key_metrics.context: What buyers pay for cash-flowing billboard assets. The speaker applies it to a board generating $96,000 a year.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the board, the operators agree that the steel is the cheap part and the government permission is the asset. Felix Finance puts it in five words, "The permit is the product," and adds that you cannot build a new one in most protected corridors [Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:01:26]. The Finance Explainer frames the same idea as "You're not buying steel, you're buying scarcity," and notes that standalone permits can trade for over a million dollars [pHu5ZfxNtfg @ 00:06:17]. Walt Runs The Numbers is blunter. The government-issued outdoor advertising permit is the thing of value, a lost permit renders your steel pole worthless, and new permits take 12 to 24 months to secure [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:01:34]. Josh Talks Business compares a capped permit to a taxi medallion. Once a jurisdiction stops issuing them, the existing ones become tradeable monopolies, and zoning plus average daily traffic decide which ones are worth owning [qH0UhNp0Now @ 00:04:39]. The consensus playbook follows from that scarcity. The 1965 Highway Beautification Act, local moratoriums, spacing rules, and four outright state bans freeze supply. An operator who already holds a legal face therefore has a moat that competitors cannot replicate by spending more on construction. The fight is over who controls the legal right to stand a sign on a high-traffic road, not over who builds the best structure.

The second point of agreement is that occupancy, not rate card, decides whether a board makes money. Josh Talks Business calls occupancy "the real machine" and argues that attention scales in a way land never does [qH0UhNp0Now @ 00:10:05]. Felix Finance repeats it almost word for word, "Occupancy rate is everything in this business," and sets the target above 85% [Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:13:01]. Walt Runs The Numbers turns that into what he calls the 85% occupancy rule, roughly 44 sold weeks a year, and underwrites every acquisition against it rather than against a full calendar [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:06:58]. ledgerandland gives the warning version: "If you underwrite a purchase at 100% of rate card, you bought a fantasy." In that speaker's numbers, real occupancy runs 70 to 85% and opex eats 25 to 40% of gross [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:16:54]. Everyone obsesses over fill because the inventory perishes. A week that passes unsold is revenue that never comes back, while the ground rent, insurance, and permit fees keep billing. The group converges on a practical rule: model at the occupancy you can prove from the seller's books, and treat anything above it as upside rather than the base case. A board that looks like a cash machine at full fill can be a slow bleed at two-thirds.

On entry strategy, the speakers line up behind buying what already exists. Profit Mechanics lays out six moves: buy an existing permit, own the land, build static and pay cash, sell ad space directly, reinvest the cash flow, and hold for ten-plus years. Chris Brown followed that sequence from one $75,000 board to roughly 30 boards in Bentonville [chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:18:31]. His second build, about $200,000 on three acres carrying eight faces, earns more than $8,000 a month, which shows land ownership compounding. Money Mechanics walks through five models (rural static, digital, premium highway, owned land, and acquisition) and flags buying existing as the recommended route [PIQPl5zhm5s @ 00:03:35]. The landowner is the silent partner in every deal. Stick to Wealth pegs ground rent at 15 to 20% of revenue, the same band Profit Mechanics and ledgerandland quote [4WZnJVbtMlk @ 00:01:24]. Once a site is locked, the consensus upgrade is digital conversion at the strongest locations. Rio Explains relays Lamar CEO Sean Reilly's numbers: a static face earning about $3,000 a month converts for roughly $200,000 and then earns $15,000 to $18,000 a month [OYv2q23Z36g @ 00:03:05]. Static is the cash-paid foundation, and digital is where operators deploy serious capital once the traffic is proven.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start with the capital stack. Walt Runs The Numbers itemizes a new highway structure: $26,000 to $45,000 for the build, another $12,000 to $18,000 for a double face, $6,000 to $15,000 for permitting, and $3,000 to $6,000 for electrical. Acquiring an existing board runs $80,000 to $250,000, which puts total entry anywhere from $60,000 to $270,000 [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:02:08]. Ned Talks Business quotes static at $15,000 to $40,000 and digital at $150,000 to $300,000, stretching to $500,000 in major markets. Ground leases in that speaker's numbers run $300 to $2,500 a month and occasionally above $5,000 [inSGoP3HxYA @ 00:01:16]. On the digital side, Felix Finance prices the LED itself at $80,000 to $250,000, notes that a P6 pixel-pitch screen costs 40% more than a P10, and puts the full digital build at $150,000 to $500,000 [Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:04:04]. Traffic sets the price of the face. ledgerandland's rule of thumb is $1,000 to $2,000 a month for every 10,000 vehicles of daily traffic [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:20:23]. That fits Felix Finance's I-10 example of 62,000 cars a day billing $9,000 a month. Ned's rate ladder fills in the rest: $200 to $500 rural, $1,000 to $3,000 suburban, and $5,000 to $20,000 prime urban.

The static P&L is thin, and every practitioner who models one shows it. Money Mechanics takes $60,000 of revenue, subtracts a $12,000 lease and $13,000 of other costs to land at $35,000, then shows a three-month vacancy deleting $15,000 of that [PIQPl5zhm5s @ 00:08:31]. Vaultonomics runs a smaller board. $3,000 a month at 75% occupancy is $27,000 a year. Subtract a $6,000 lease, roughly $4,000 in 15% commissions, and $4,000 of operating costs, and about $13,000 remains, enough to pay back a $70,000 build in five to six years [clsOKO3QgiM @ 00:07:15]. Econometrics finds the floor with a $40,000 board sold at $2,000 per four-week block across 13 blocks. It breaks even near 38% fill and loses about $800 at 35%, while 65% fill clears roughly $6,200 for a 6.5-year payback [q9ejuh31AvI @ 00:03:20]. Leverage squeezes the margin further. Walt Runs The Numbers takes a $3,500-a-month board to $1,760 to $1,955 of monthly NOI. Borrowing $120,000 at 8.5% over ten years then eats about $1,048 a month, leaving only $275 to $470 [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:03:53]. That math explains the pay-cash rule in the six-move playbook.

Digital changes the inventory math because one structure is sold many times over. ledgerandland's worked example starts with a static board grossing $72,000 and netting about $41,000. After conversion, the same site grosses $230,400, carries roughly $110,000 of opex, and nets about $120,000, close to three times the static net [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:17:38]. Money Mechanics shows how slot fill swings the result. A $300,000 build with eight slots at $2,500 a month grosses $240,000 a year, but filling only six of eight drops that to $180,000 [PIQPl5zhm5s @ 00:09:34]. Rio Explains cites analyst estimates of roughly a 43% return on Lamar conversions after a 20% lease and a 7% commission, and says Lamar converts 300 to 500 faces a year [OYv2q23Z36g @ 00:03:57]. The exit math makes the slow burn worth it. Profit Mechanics says buyers pay seven to twelve times revenue, so a board generating $96,000 a year prices at roughly $670,000 to more than $1 million [chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:22:10]. On those numbers, operators who scale static faces, convert their best sites, and hold occupancy above 85% are building an asset priced on a multiple, not just collecting rent from a pole beside the highway.

callout.title: Margin Levers the Operators Actually Pull
callout.body: These four moves came up repeatedly as the difference between a board that pays and a board that bleeds slowly.
items: Watch the discount trap. A one-off $1,500 deal still contributes $1,350, but if discounting becomes the norm the board needs roughly 87% fill to hold its economics [Econometrics — q9ejuh31AvI @ 00:05:16].

Cap lease escalators at 2-3% when negotiating ground leases of 10 to 25 years, and stagger lease expirations across the portfolio so they do not all reset at once [Felix Finance — Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:05:04].
Day-part digital slots: coffee in the morning, restaurants in the evening. With 6-10 slots on an 8-second rotation, this drives a 4-10x gross multiplier [Hidden Economics — XlZ7pkhH2fM @ 00:02:17].

Sell direct, because direct sales carry the highest margin compared with agencies and programmatic. Keep the creative to 7-8 words maximum to suit dwell time and read distance [The Finance Explainer — pHu5ZfxNtfg @ 00:06:59].

sop_steps.title: Confirm the Permit Before the Steel
sop_steps.action: Verify a legal, transferable permit and a secured site before committing any construction or purchase capital.
sop_steps.detail: Building before the permit is confirmed is one of the biggest beginner mistakes. If the location is not legal, you end up holding a very expensive pole. New permits take 12 to 24 months, so buying an existing permitted structure skips that wait [Global Finance Desk — AkX52_z30r4 @ 00:09:27].

sop_steps.title: Price the Face Off Traffic
sop_steps.action: Pull daily traffic counts and set the rate card using the per-10,000-vehicle rule.
sop_steps.detail: Charge $1,000 to $2,000 a month for every 10,000 vehicles of daily traffic. Roads carrying 50,000 to 150,000 vehicles a day support bulletin pricing [ledgerandland — 6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:20:23].

sop_steps.title: Underwrite at 85%, Then Stress Below It
sop_steps.action: Model revenue at 85% occupancy (44 weeks), then rerun the model at the breakeven fill rate.
sop_steps.detail: Use the 85% occupancy rule as the base case [Walt Runs The Numbers — 9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:06:58]. Then confirm where the board breaks even: about 38% fill on a $40,000 static build, with a loss of roughly $800 at 35% [Econometrics — q9ejuh31AvI @ 00:03:20].

sop_steps.title: Ride the Boards, Then Hire Reps
sop_steps.action: Sell the inventory personally until the portfolio reaches about 15-20 faces, then add commissioned reps.
sop_steps.detail: The owner sells directly until roughly 15-20 faces, then hires reps at 10-20% commission. Target more than 85% occupancy, and backfill unsold time with programmatic at $8-15 CPM [Felix Finance — Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:12:42].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The build-versus-buy split is the first fork, and the operators land on opposite sides of the cost sheet. Profit Mechanics lays out a six-move ladder that starts with buying an existing permit, owning the land, building static paid in cash, selling direct, reinvesting, and holding ten-plus years [chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:18:31]. Money Mechanics runs five models side by side and still recommends buying existing over rural static, digital, premium highway, or owned-land plays, pricing a fresh build at roughly $145K all-in [PIQPl5zhm5s @ 00:14:00]. Walt Runs The Numbers breaks a ground-up job into $26-45K of structure, $6-15K of permitting, and $3-6K of electrical, against $80-250K to acquire a standing board, for total entry anywhere from $60K to $270K [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:02:08]. Ledgerandland goes harder and files new-build fantasy as one of seven traps, right alongside lease expiry, eminent domain, and no-rebuild rules [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:21:21]. The pattern is consistent across the cost sheets: the operators who buy permits talk about cash flow from day one, and the operators who build talk about steel, permitting calendars, and electrical hookups long before the first advertiser signs a contract. That timing gap, more than the steel itself, is what separates the two camps on paper.

Digital conversion is where the payback math splits widest, and the spread is not a rounding error. Felix Finance claims converting an $8K-a-month face to $30K costs $200K and pays back in nine months [Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:10:57]. The Finance Explainer runs a far tamer case: a $200K digital build sold as eight slots at $600 each, or $4,800 a month, clearing $3-10K of monthly profit with a two-to-three-year payback [pHu5ZfxNtfg @ 00:14:10]. Profit Mechanics stretches the payback further to three to five years even while crediting digital with four to six times static revenue across six to eight rotating advertisers [chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:05:55]. Ledgerandland's worked example shows why the camps diverge: a $72K static gross producing about $41K of NOI becomes $230,400 gross after conversion, but roughly $110K of opex eats in and leaves about $120K NOI, which is 'three times net' rather than the headline gross multiple [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:17:38]. Across these operators, quoted payback runs from nine months to five years on similar six-figure checks. The disagreement is mostly about what gets counted. The optimists quote gross lift on a prime face; the conservative operators load power, slot vacancy, and screen aging into the opex line before they let themselves call the upgrade a win.

Cash versus leverage is the sharpest philosophical split. Profit Mechanics' Chris Brown paid $75,000 for structure plus land with no debt, two faces at $600 a month each, and the ladder he teaches insists on building static paid in cash [chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:01:41]. Josh Talks Business takes the opposite line: borrow against the land, the permit, and projected revenue, with the blunt caveat that 'the bank gets paid first' [qH0UhNp0Now @ 00:07:14]. Ned Talks Business shows what leverage looks like at scale: a $4.2M purchase throwing off $1.1M of revenue against roughly $730K of costs and $288K of debt service, netting about $109K yet projected to a 20-25% IRR [inSGoP3HxYA @ 00:15:50]. Walt Runs The Numbers runs the single-board version and the margin almost disappears: $3,500 a month, NOI of $1,760-1,955, then about $1,048 of debt service on $120K at 8.5% over ten years leaves only $275-470 a month [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:03:53]. Note Brown's own figures drift: $2,400 a month early, $2,800 in the recap, so even the cash camp's headline number needs a recount. The operator takeaway is that debt converts a comfortable board into a thin one, and the IRR story only works when the revenue line holds.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Vacancy is the failure mode every operator has paid for in real dollars. Walt Runs The Numbers walks through an Oklahoma case: a $185K purchase, a four-month vacancy that cost $16,200, an $8,400 storm repair, and $29K lost by month eighteen [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:08:41]. Money Mechanics prices the same pain on a smaller board, where a $60K revenue line minus a $12K lease and $13K of other costs leaves $35K, and a three-month vacancy wipes out $15K of it [PIQPl5zhm5s @ 00:08:31]. Econometrics shows how thin the floor is: a $40K build selling $2,000 four-week blocks breaks even near 38% fill, loses about $800 at 35%, and a $1,500 discount that becomes the norm pushes the required fill to roughly 87% [q9ejuh31AvI @ 00:03:20]. Ledgerandland puts the underwriting rule bluntly: 'If you underwrite a purchase at 100% of rate card, you bought a fantasy' [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:16:54]. Every unsold period is unrecoverable inventory, which is why discounting to fill a gap feels safe in the moment but quietly resets the whole rate card downward. The fix the operators converge on is to underwrite at realistic occupancy, model a multi-month dark stretch in year one, and refuse to let a one-off discount become the posted price.

Permit risk is the trap that turns steel into scrap. Global Finance Desk names building before the permit is confirmed, signing a weak lease, and choosing cheap land over traffic as the classic beginner mistakes, and sums up the result in one line: 'Now you have a very expensive pole' [AkX52_z30r4 @ 00:09:27]. Walt Runs The Numbers is just as flat about it: 'A lost permit renders your steel pole worthless' [9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:08:06]. Ledgerandland adds the slower-moving version of the same loss: signs destroyed past a damage threshold cannot be rebuilt, which means one heavy damage event can convert a grandfathered location into an empty lot [6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:06:55]. Follow the Fee explains why there is no workaround once supply is locked: moratoriums and spacing rules cap inventory, Oregon's cap-and-replace system demands three static boards removed for a single trivision unit, and 'You cannot build your way into a moratorium' [lQ0ni5KmJiE @ 00:09:09]. The practical consequence is that the permit, not the structure, is the asset being underwritten. Operators who treat paperwork as an afterthought end up holding hardware with no legal right to display anything, while operators who verify permit status, lease terms, and rebuild limits before closing keep the scarcity value intact.

Debt and ad cycles are the traps that hit the biggest names hardest. Profit Mechanics puts Clear Channel Outdoor at $5.6B of debt, roughly 12 times cash flow, with about $420M a year of interest, against the 2-4 times a healthy business carries [chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:15:29]. Follow the Fee traces how it got there: a roughly $27B leveraged buyout that pushed debt from $8B to more than $20B, iHeart's Chapter 11 in 2018, and European exits for $625M and about $135M [lQ0ni5KmJiE @ 00:17:58]. Stick to Wealth frames the lesson in one line: 'The house can be a money machine and the mortgage can still crush you' [4WZnJVbtMlk @ 00:05:00]. MoneyLogics shows how fast the revenue side can break: Clear Channel Outdoor Americas revenue fell 39% in Q2 2020, and 'The customers just vanished' [8Emqeya9KGo @ 00:01:39]. Put those together and the failure mode is not a bad billboard; it is a good billboard carrying a capital structure that cannot survive a single bad quarter. Scarce locations do not pay lenders when advertisers stop buying. Small operators should run their own debt service against a sudden revenue drop before signing a loan, and size the note so the boards still clear interest in a down year.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Billboard Deal Closes
callout.body: Every check below comes from a loss an operator actually reported: steel without a permit, rate-card fantasy, lease creep, and debt that outran the boards.
items: Confirm the permit before any steel goes up; building first is how beginners end up with 'a very expensive pole' [Global Finance Desk — AkX52_z30r4 @ 00:09:45].
Underwrite occupancy at the 85% rule, roughly 44 sold weeks, never at full rate card [Walt Runs The Numbers — 9d5MJAQGDk8 @ 00:06:58].
Read the ground lease for right-of-first-refusal and tear-down clauses before pricing the board [ledgerandland — 6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:10:33].
Stress-test interest at 6% versus 9% and refuse to enter undercapitalized at $20K [Money Mechanics — PIQPl5zhm5s @ 00:21:27].

action_checklist: Run revenue as traffic x price per face x filled faces before making any offer [Profit Mechanics — chCNj5IEUZw @ 00:08:25].
Price each face off traffic at $1-2K per month per 10K vehicles of daily traffic [ledgerandland — 6oamhwKj2wU @ 00:20:23].
Value a board as net income divided by an 8-10% cap rate, e.g., $10K at 8% equals $125K [Hidden Economics — XlZ7pkhH2fM @ 00:04:19].
Ride the boards yourself until about 15-20 faces, then hire reps at 10-20% commission and target over 85% occupancy [Felix Finance — Zfn3IARm5no @ 00:12:42].
Budget vinyl at $200-500 per change plus $100-300 for install before quoting margin [Ned Talks Business — inSGoP3HxYA @ 00:06:59].
Aim digital upgrades only at the strongest sites, measured by daily effective circulation such as 100,000 vehicles [Global Finance Desk — AkX52_z30r4 @ 00:06:31].

chapters.question_prompt: How do billboard operators sell ad space, and do digital, mobile and indoor formats change the business?
chapters.title: Selling the Face: Billboard Ad Sales and New Formats
chapters.subtitle: Consultative selling, audience-based pricing, the math of billboard ROI for advertisers, renting the same face to many advertisers, digital billboard economics, Blip, $250K LED mobile trucks, and indoor billboards
chapters.executive_summary: Operators across static, digital, mobile, indoor and programmatic formats agree the face is sold on location, rate and occupancy, not on steel. Behind The Billions ranks panels by revenue per panel, from $3-8K rural to $300K-plus digital corridors; The Bell Board Podcast's Jonathan Graviss targets 75-80% occupancy before pushing rate and puts a double-commission bounty on boards empty 90 days. Tasty Ad wins contracts by showing spec ads before signing. Street numbers: a digital face earns $144K versus $36K static in the Billboard Insider model, Blip clears around 2-6 cents per blip, LED trucks book $1,200-3,600 a day, and indoor screens carry 5-10 advertisers at $100-300 a month. Practitioners split on digital rotation counts, on whether billboards still undercut Meta and Google on CPM, and on whether beginners should start static.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across static, digital and programmatic sellers, the face is treated as rented attention sitting on a permitted piece of ground. The Money Mindset HQ frames the business as "renting out eyeballs," priced off daily effective circulation, and states flatly that "the permission to have a board there is the asset," because the 1965 Highway Beautification Act turned legal sites into grandfathered monopolies [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:00:36] [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:09:44]. The Mister Finance makes the same point from the structure side: one structure carries two faces, each sold independently, and the operator is reselling access to the location rather than the steel itself [g_IGLl-xq-I @ 00:01:07]. Behind The Billions turns that logic into a revenue ladder: rural panels pull $3-8K, suburban $10-20K, urban interstate $50-200K, and a digital premium corridor $300K-plus [Bb-6A1zEJAc @ 00:03:26]. For a seller, the consensus is that the price ceiling is fixed before the first prospecting call goes out. Traffic count, audience fit, sight angle and legal standing decide what a face can command. The sales job is to fill that face at the highest rate the location supports, across as many weeks of the year as possible, without trading the panel away below what the location is actually worth to an advertiser.

Practitioners also agree that nobody buys a face sight unseen, and nobody renews one they cannot measure. Tasty Ad compares billboard selling to a car lot where no buyer signs before seeing the vehicle, then calls out reps who show up with a contract, a map and photos but no creative; the fix is a spec ad in front of every prospect and every renewal before the contract comes out [ivfNhpDax7I @ 00:00:53]. Adrian Boysel says 9 out of 10 billboards blow the message itself, leading with a logo when the reader wants WIIFM, what's in it for me, and points to the Somerset Assisted Living board, where the logo eats three quarters of the face and "nobody cares"; the call to action, whether a QR code, phone number or URL, has to be big [14aRU-ObgC0 @ 00:05:27]. On proof, Jared VanderMeer warns that billboards are hard to track and tells buyers to run a unique URL or phone number [NtQMMoZo6dw @ 00:03:56], while Boysel stacks a dedicated landing page, QR retargeting, call tracking, an SMS short code such as "text roof to 45456," and a simple where-did-you-hear-about-us question on every inbound call [14aRU-ObgC0 @ 00:09:01]. Creative and attribution are part of the sale, not an afterthought.

The third point of agreement is that a face earns on duration and fill, so occupancy discipline sits at the center of every sales operation, static or digital. Jonathan Graviss of The Bell Board Podcast sets the working target at 75-80% occupancy: above that band the team pushes rate, and below it the team pushes occupancy until the inventory fills back up [N6EyLPQ9NhA @ 00:25:03]. The Money Mindset HQ sets a higher 80-90% target and notes that programmatic fill can backstop empty time from roughly 15 cents [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:10:01]. The Mister Finance tells sellers to track occupancy face by face and to take a lower price from a long-term advertiser rather than lose weeks of revenue to an empty board, running the whole desk off a rate card, booking calendar, contracts and collections, and never promising an advertiser purchases [g_IGLl-xq-I @ 00:10:24]. Billboard Source sells on the same clock: the minimum stay is usually 3 months, 6 or 12 months is typical, and anything shorter counts as a short-term buy that carries a premium for events and promotions [gReq9TXl5BY @ 00:01:18]. Read together, the operating floor is a full calendar of paying advertisers, and the premium only gets charged once that calendar is mostly sold.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The street pitch starts with intake and spec creative. Billboard Source runs every inquiry like a hotel booking in four steps: check-in date, whether that is ASAP or a seasonal push; length of stay; room type, meaning highway boards for broad awareness or specific units for a target demographic; and budget, the step it calls most important, given as a range such as $10,000 versus $100,000 [gReq9TXl5BY @ 00:00:41]. From there it sends available boards with maps, reserves the space on contract, designs in-house for free and handles printing and installation. Tasty Ad attacks the slowest link in that chain: reps either wait 3 days for spec art or pay an outrageous fee without an in-house designer, so its tool builds ads in minutes with no design skills, backed by its own network of 23 digital displays at 95%-plus occupancy with a small sales staff [ivfNhpDax7I @ 00:01:09]. Inside the sales team, Graviss reviews unsold inventory and pays a bounty of double commission on any board sitting empty 90 days [N6EyLPQ9NhA @ 00:13:11], and uses AI to draft letters to the owners of 16-17 sites in about 30 minutes [N6EyLPQ9NhA @ 00:32:51]. Speed to creative and speed to outreach are the two levers the sharpest sellers pull.

Pricing runs on cost per impression, and the sellers who close show their math on paper before a buyer ever sees a contract. Jared VanderMeer divides a $1,000-a-month board by 50,000 viewers to land at 2 cents per impression, then tells buyers to hold that number against digital channels at the negotiating table, since billboards have stayed in the 2-5 cent band while digital costs climb [NtQMMoZo6dw @ 00:01:27]. The Money Mindset HQ works the same math: $3,300 divided by 1.4 million impressions comes out near a $2.36 CPM, inside a standard range of $2-18, with premium faces at $15-25-plus and premium digital at $30-80 [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:03:19]. Rents are typically sold in 4-week blocks, from $250 to $14K for static and $1.2K to $15K for digital, and a Geopath-certified daily effective circulation of 80K commands 40-60% more than an uncertified board [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:01:32]. Adrian Boysel prices boards at $5,000 to $35,000 a month, with Sunset Boulevard at $15K-35K, production at $250-1,500 and installation on top [14aRU-ObgC0 @ 00:10:15]. The pattern is consistent: quote rate as a CPM, anchor it to the buyer's digital spend, and get the audience number certified so the rate holds up when the buyer pushes back on price at renewal.

The newer formats sell the face by the day, the slot or the six-second play. Blip, walked through by Bart Bradshaw on Local Marketing Institute, has a one-cent minimum, advertisers running $5 to $50-plus a day, and a worked example of $25 a day equaling $750 a month; the default bid is $0.35 per blip, but Bradshaw bids $0.50 because "our algorithm favors the higher" bid, and observed clearing costs run about 2-6 cents per 6-8 second blip [uoJvU0CyoBY @ 00:48:29]. Campaigns go from location, budget, schedule and artwork to review and launch, live within 24-48 hours after Blip and operator moderation [uoJvU0CyoBY @ 00:38:14]. On wheels, Cant Miss US prices route campaigns at $1,200-1,800 a day and tailgates, festivals and political rallies at $2,500-3,600 a day, so 10 event days a month grosses $12K-18K [o3KgQJFdGXQ @ 00:01:10]. Indoors, Hustle Labs places a free screen in a partner business with long dwell time, offers the owner content management plus a 20-30% revenue share, then sells 5-10 ad slots per screen at $100-300 a month each; five advertisers at $150 is $750 a month from one screen [IsQBWJcu3ro @ 00:04:53]. Each format trades permanence for speed, and each lives or dies on how many slots stay sold.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is static versus digital, and it starts with how many advertisers one screen really carries. Behind The Billions models 8 to 12 ads per minute and treats conversion as a $200K to $500K spend that pays back in 2 to 3 years while lifting a site's value from $200K to $1M [Bb-6A1zEJAc @ 00:07:21]. Ekoniq cites Broadsign at only 4 to 5 ads per 60 seconds, yet still shows the same board jumping from $36K static to $144K digital, a 4x lift [eI1lH8lhvd8 @ 00:06:40]. Ekoniq also models a standard 14x48 conversion at roughly $200K, so that lift has to cover a large check. The Mister Finance pushes back hard: more advertising slots do not automatically mean more profit, so beginners should start with static and earn their way into screens [g_IGLl-xq-I @ 00:09:12]. Finpulse puts that warning into numbers. Eight rotating ads do not mean eight times the profit, and a six-slot face at $1,500 per slot grosses $9,000 only when every slot sells, collapsing to $4,500 when just three do [WCGRAxsks5U @ 00:07:13]. Digital multiplies inventory; it does not multiply buyers, and the rotation count each camp quotes changes the slot math before a single contract is signed.

The second fight is whether outdoor is still cheap. Jared VanderMeer runs the math as $1,000 a month divided by 50,000 viewers, or 2 cents per impression, and argues billboards hold steady at 2 to 5 cents while digital channel costs keep rising, making cost per impression the lever to pull in any negotiation [NtQMMoZo6dw @ 00:03:04]. Jonathan Graviss on The Bell Board Podcast disputes the premise: Meta and Google now match outdoor's CPM, outdoor has held roughly 5% of media share for decades, and Graviss's rapid-fire answers call the claim that digital is overpriced false [N6EyLPQ9NhA @ 00:40:41]. The same split shows up inside the sales office. Graviss sets 75 to 80% occupancy as the hinge, pushing rate above it and occupancy below it, while host Neil Bell leans occupancy-first [N6EyLPQ9NhA @ 00:25:03]. The Money Mindset HQ pushes the target higher, aiming for 80 to 90% occupancy and backfilling open slots with programmatic fill starting around 15 cents [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:10:01]. Graviss also attacks dead inventory directly with a bounty of double commission on any board sitting empty 90 days and a standing review of unsold faces. As the Bell Board conversation puts it, you have to take advantage of rate and occupancy.

The third divide is format and contract length. Billboard Source sells like a hotel booking: a 3-month minimum, 6 or 12 months typical, a premium for anything shorter, and free in-house design once the contract reserves the space [gReq9TXl5BY @ 00:01:18]. Blip's Bart Bradshaw tears that model up, selling digital faces by the blip with a one-cent minimum, advertisers spending $5 to $50+ a day, and campaigns live within 24 to 48 hours after Blip and operator moderation [uoJvU0CyoBY @ 00:38:33]. Traditional digital contracts, per the Blip team, run about four weeks to half a year at $1,000 to $20,000+, and traditional advertisers make up only about 2% of the market. On wheels, the camps split again. Jerry Teeter of Mobile Digital Billboard University pitches a $250K Legion 613 truck plus a business-in-a-box kit of manuals, contracts, website and media-kit templates [mG9J2Z6RgSY @ 00:07:05]. Cant Miss US answers the passive-income question with a flat no, calling the truck a high-tech mobile media asset instead, with route days at $1,200 to $1,800 and event days at $2,500 to $3,600 [o3KgQJFdGXQ @ 00:01:32]. Both camps sell trucks, and Cant Miss US openly pitches buying from a proven fleet for the support system, not just the metal.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures are lease and leverage failures, not bad creative. Behind The Billions walks through a buyer who paid $400M for 300 boards with 75% debt, watched ground leases come back at double rent, and went bankrupt in 2021, then a $30M digital program where 60% of leases expired, rents rose 40 to 80%, and the network sold at a loss in 2023 [Bb-6A1zEJAc @ 00:07:54]. The root paradox is that a $20K structure depreciates over 40 years while the ground lease under it renews every 20. The Money Mindset HQ quantifies the squeeze: a 10-point rent rise costs about 18% of cash flow, so lock fixed 2 to 3% escalators and a minimum rent, and know that easements sell for 8 to 15 times rent [JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:11:14]. The Mister Finance flags the earlier trap of signing a long lease before approvals and paying rent where you are legally unable to build, and warns that grandfathered sites may not be rebuildable [g_IGLl-xq-I @ 00:03:41]. How They Make Money lists the standing risks every operator carries: sign-code changes, losing a lease, recessions and storms [eVhqvVbf0rA @ 00:03:25]. Lease cost is no rounding error either: Outfront carries about $447M in lease costs against roughly $1.39B in billboard revenue.

Digital boards fail quietly through leaks and empty slots. Ekoniq itemizes the drains: about $12K a year in electricity, percentage-of-gross leases, sales cost, maintenance and software [eI1lH8lhvd8 @ 00:07:20]. Its list of common mistakes reads like a site-selection autopsy: building a second face, road reroutes, buildings going up in front of the board, and putting a third digital board in the same mile [eI1lH8lhvd8 @ 00:08:55]. Even the small-market case Ekoniq models is modest: $80K of capital, 65% occupancy, $35,100 in revenue, $26,790 EBITDA and a 24% return. The Mister Finance shows how fast occupancy flips the sign: 10 boards and 20 faces at $1,800 per 4 weeks and 70% occupancy gross $327,600 a year and clear about $4,300 a month after $23K of monthly expenses, but at 50% occupancy the same network bleeds $3,500 a month on roughly $850K of construction [g_IGLl-xq-I @ 00:20:19]. That is why The Mister Finance insists each face be measured individually and expansion follow verified cash flow and legal rights, not excitement. Finpulse adds that permits and zoning create a barrier to entry but no guaranteed monopoly [WCGRAxsks5U @ 00:08:28]. The math lesson is identical across all three: model the face at realistic fill, not full rotation.

On the street, deals die from sloppy execution. Tasty Ad says reps walk in with a contract, map and photos but no creative, and that the bottleneck is spec art taking 3 days or costing an outrageous fee without an in-house designer, so spec ads belong in front of every prospect and every renewal before the contract [ivfNhpDax7I @ 00:01:09]. Tasty Ad backs the fix with its own network: 95%+ occupancy across 23 digital displays after nearly a decade with a small sales staff. Adrian Boysel says 9 out of 10 billboards get messaging wrong, even calling out their own Somerset Assisted Living logo, which fills three-quarters of the board, because nobody cares, and warns that a bad location can mean zero return and that expecting month one to fund month two ignores the 13-exposure, 13-week minimum [14aRU-ObgC0 @ 00:05:27]. On mobile, Jerry Teeter says most trucks are underpowered on 8, 10 or 12 kW generators, specifying 20 kW and a sealed cab wall because aging generators leak carbon monoxide [mG9J2Z6RgSY @ 00:02:56]. Hustle Labs lists the indoor version: buying 10 screens on day one, chasing trendy locations over measured dwell time, and undercharging, and assigns pitching three high-traffic businesses this week as the first move [IsQBWJcu3ro @ 00:07:00].

callout.title: Four Hard Stops Before Signing Ground, Steel or Screens
callout.body: Each stop below maps to a loss or trap a named practitioner reported. If any one fails, the deal waits.
items: No long ground lease until approvals clear and permits are verified transferable; otherwise you pay rent where you are legally unable to build [The Mister Finance — g_IGLl-xq-I @ 00:03:41].
No leveraged acquisition without modeling lease renewals at double rent, the exact scenario that bankrupted a 300-board, 75%-debt roll-up in 2021 [Behind The Billions — Bb-6A1zEJAc @ 00:07:54].
No digital conversion until the face works at realistic fill: three of six slots sold at $1,500 halves gross from $9,000 to $4,500 [Finpulse — WCGRAxsks5U @ 00:07:13].

No campaign launch without tracking: a dedicated URL or landing page, QR retargeting, call tracking, an SMS short code, and asking callers where they heard of you [Adrian Boysel — 14aRU-ObgC0 @ 00:09:01].

action_checklist: Build spec ads and put them in front of every prospect and every renewal before the contract comes out [Tasty Ad — ivfNhpDax7I @ 00:00:53].
Run cost per impression (monthly cost divided by viewers) and compare it against digital channels when negotiating a board [Jared VanderMeer — NtQMMoZo6dw @ 00:04:54].
Review unsold inventory and post a double-commission bounty on any board that has sat empty for 90 days [The Bell Board Podcast — N6EyLPQ9NhA @ 00:13:11].
Lock fixed 2 to 3% escalators and a minimum rent so a 10-point rent rise cannot strip about 18% of cash flow [The Money Mindset HQ — JCnJw5eFyEE @ 00:11:14].
Qualify every buyer on start date, length of stay, board type and a budget range such as $10,000 versus $100,000 [Billboard Source — gReq9TXl5BY @ 00:02:11].
On pay-per-blip buys, bid above the $0.35 default; Bart Bradshaw bids $0.50 because the algorithm favors the higher bid [Local Marketing Institute — uoJvU0CyoBY @ 00:48:29].

chapters.question_prompt: What is industrial outdoor storage, why is institutional capital chasing it, and what makes a good IOS site?
chapters.title: Industrial Outdoor Storage: The Asset Class and the Market
chapters.subtitle: IOS definitions and macro trends, perfect-site criteria and pre-purchase checks, Florida and Inland Empire yards, the $4.8M Fontana deal, equipment rental net lease vs. IOS, financing, and the institutional surge (CBRE, NAIOP)
chapters.executive_summary: IOS operators agree that the land, the zoning, and the tenants are the asset. Buildings cover under 10 to 25 percent of the site and barely need underwriting. Zoning is the dominant risk; Alterra's Leo Addimando ranks it number one through five, and grandfathered non-conforming uses are the classic trap. National IOS vacancy sits at 2.5 percent versus 6.7 percent for traditional industrial, and market rent runs 29.8 percent above in-place rent. On the street, users want 1 to 3 acres, site work runs $75,000 to $300,000 per acre, and a 2-acre site can shrink to 1.5 usable acres. Ned of 9606 Capital buys Atlanta at 8.5 percent against 7 percent stabilized trades, and lenders want a 10 percent debt yield and 1.25x DSCR. The split is demand depth: Industrial Advisors calls it overstated for 5 to 7 acre sites, while institutional players report leasing has never been busier.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator starts from the same premise: in industrial outdoor storage the dirt, not the building, is the asset. Ryan Solberg of MaxLife frames it bluntly, saying that with IOS “there is barely a building to underwrite” and that the value sits in the land, the zoning, and tenants who cannot park a truck anywhere else [oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:00:40]. Chase MacLeod defines the product as an industrial property with substantially more outside yard than building, with coverage typically under 10 to 25 percent; on 3 acres, roughly 130,000 SF, a good building runs about 15,000 to 20,000 SF, and some yards have no building at all [m96MC6Qe9oM @ 00:00:15]. Edison Basquez of EdisonIndustrial calls it “a small building on a large piece of land” [-7jTPPttg2s @ 00:00:29], and the Dolphin speaker on CREDA Global's NAIOP segment says the value comes from the land rent, with lower coverage used to store equipment, vehicles, and building materials [cKtqug8KPPk @ 00:00:03]. The tenant roster is consistent across the field: logistics firms, 3PLs, construction firms, fleet managers, container users, trailer storage, equipment rental, and pallet operators. Solberg's warning is the takeaway: investors who carry a warehouse checklist to a truck yard miss the items that actually decide the deal.

The loudest point of agreement is zoning. Leo Addimando of Alterra, speaking on CBRE's program, ranks zoning as risk “number one… through five,” says commercial zoning does not work, and treats illegal truck parking on a site as a warning sign [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:17:20]. The Dolphin speaker on CREDA Global's NAIOP segment names the top three underwriting challenges as “zoning, zoning, and zoning” and hires local land-use counsel on every acquisition [cKtqug8KPPk @ 00:00:58]. Steve Azar of Ambient Capital Partners runs in-house land-use expertise that goes deeper than the zoning report, warning that a buyer must confirm the site is not “just a grandfathered legal non-conforming use that's going to go away when the tenant goes away,” and noting that Southern California towns are cracking down on non-conforming sites [znP8wX2_k2w @ 00:12:40]. Justin Horowitz of Cooper Horowitz adds the buyer-side wrinkle: a seller's municipal ties can hide zoning limits, so hire zoning counsel instead of leaning on the seller's comfort [yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:15:16]. The upside of a clean entitlement is optionality. Addimando says over 95 percent of Alterra's sites could support vertical industrial, but not the inverse. None of these operators treats zoning as a post-closing question.

The demand-side numbers line up across national sources. Commercial Real Estate Now cites CBRE's Q4 2025 national IOS vacancy of 2.5 percent against 6.7 percent for traditional industrial, with market rent 29.8 percent above in-place rent in Q1 2026, the widest mark-to-market gap of any industrial segment [dKQj8cpiqeE @ 00:01:53]. Steve Azar puts quality IOS vacancy near 2 percent versus near-double-digit vacancy for industrial broadly, says IOS nationally runs half the warehouse vacancy with twice the rent growth, and reports leasing has never been busier on the back of AI buildout demand [znP8wX2_k2w @ 00:11:42]. Leo Addimando sizes the universe at $200 billion to $500 billion with under 10 percent institutionally owned, while CBRE's Will Pike says every major industrial allocator now has an IOS strategy and the sector was recently added to NCREIF [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:15:15]. Jonathan Gonzalez of Capright lists what institutionalization brings: greater scale, more transactions and larger portfolios, more operating data, standardized leases, timely reporting, and pricing transparency that helps the asset class mature [p8t7CLKouHw @ 00:00:20]. The shared baseline is by-right zoning, a functional yard, and location. Addimando places Alterra's sites 3 to 5 miles from a port, interstate, intermodal hub, or airport, and puts tenant costs at 50 percent transportation and under 5 percent occupancy.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The physical spec is tight and numeric. Edison Basquez says the perfect site for most users is under 5 acres, ideally 1 to 3, with a 10,000 to 20,000 SF building on 2 to 5 acres, multi-tenant divisibility, and real infrastructure, because gravel alone fails: municipalities require paving, drainage, fencing, and lighting before tenants or owners can get business licenses [-7jTPPttg2s @ 00:00:53]. Ned of 9606 Capital buys broader. Coverage under 10 percent always works and under 20 percent can work depending on layout, with buildings of 3,000 to 50,000 SF on 3 to 25 acres. The 9606 site-work numbers run $75,000 to $125,000 per acre for light work and $175,000 to $300,000 for heavy work, with Jacksonville near $225,000 and Chicago near $125,000 per acre [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:29:59]. Matt McGregor of Industrial Advisors pegs typical capex at 9 to 18 inches of crushed rock or paving, with near-zero cost between tenants [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:01:35]. The usable-acre haircut is the number buyers forget. EdisonIndustrial shows a 2-acre site losing 0.5 acre to landscaping, retention, and setbacks, leaving 1.5 usable acres, and tenants may pay only on the usable area [Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:02:33]. Price the land you can actually rent, not the acreage on the deed.

Rent and pricing quotes vary by market, and the operators give them straight. Ryan Solberg offers Florida planning ranges, not quotes: cap rates of about 6.75 to 8 percent, with paved, secured I-4 corridor sites trading toward the tighter end, rents of $40,000 to $90,000 per acre per year, and roughly 150 to 200 basis points of compression [oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:02:34]. Ned traces Atlanta rents from $1,200 to $1,500 to $1,800 and then $4,000 per acre per month, now about $5,000. Stabilized assets trade at a 7 cap, and Ned buys at 8.5 percent, a 150-basis-point discount, after modeling 6 to 8 months of vacancy [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:14:54]. Horowitz quotes New Jersey rents of $25,000 to $30,000 per acre per month in Newark and $15,000 to $20,000 in secondary markets, plus an entry play in Mobile at $2,000 per acre per month on a 15-year lease with 3 percent bumps [yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:11:48]. Commercial Real Estate Now pegs primary-market caps at 6 to 6.75 percent and secondary at 6.75 to 7.75 percent. IOS leases run 2 to 5 years with 10 to 15 percent bumps at renewal, against 15-year net leases with 10 percent escalations every 5 years [dKQj8cpiqeE @ 00:03:54].

Debt is where the mechanics get exact. Horowitz underwrites to a 10 percent debt yield and 1.25x DSCR. Managed truck parking needs a 12 to 13 percent debt yield and prices in the high-6s to low-7s, roughly a 50-basis-point premium; Horowitz calls it “like a hotel.” The Elkridge, Maryland United Rentals deal went 10-year fixed at 6.8 percent, roughly 6.5 percent today, and $25 million to $200 million portfolios price at high-1s to low-2s over Treasuries [yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:21:12]. Ned reports banks now want global cash flow. Against the banks' 1.25 requirement, Ned's DSCR sits at 2.6, and leverage across everything 9606 Capital owns is under 35 percent [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:24:12]. Solberg points buyers to specialized lenders, life companies, or debt funds at about 60 to 70 percent LTV, with SBA 504 possible for owner-users [oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:04:59]. Addimando puts IOS borrowing costs “about 50 basis points wide” and valuation spreads to traditional industrial at 25 to 50 basis points, narrowed from 150. Addimando also forecasts borrowing costs and cap rates converging with traditional industrial within five years [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:12:36]. Rate locks swing fast: Horowitz saw a 6.29 percent lock that would have been 6.24 percent a week later and 6.40 percent two weeks later, and expects roughly 20-basis-point swings.

callout.title: Street-Level Moves the Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Four tactics pulled straight from operators who entitle, build out, lease, and tour IOS yards for a living.
items: Never pitch it as a truck terminal: Steve Sprenger calls it a “high throughput logistics freight facility,” because cities want employee counts on a site with only about 20 percent building coverage [Adding Value w/ Shy Assar | CRE & Industrial — tn1QmPINHeE @ 00:15:29].
Watch the base-material math: Ned reports gravel at $800 per truck, while asphalt millings come in at $30 per truck versus a $50 dump fee [Industrial Real Estate Show — LftC_mcL69E @ 00:29:41].

Rent by the stall when a yard will not lease whole: Matt McGregor rents per-trailer stalls at about $250 with a 10-stall minimum, while admitting it is hard to manage [Industrial Advisors — gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:05:23].
Run the 53-footer test on every tour: Justin Horowitz tours every site and checks whether a 53-foot trailer can turn in [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:06:44].

sop_steps.title: Lock the Zoning Before Anything Else
sop_steps.action: Verify with the city that the zoning allows outdoor storage by-right, and price what it costs to make the site compliant.
sop_steps.detail: EdisonIndustrial warns that industrial zoning may not allow outdoor storage and that buyers have bought non-compliant sites, so find out what compliance takes and costs before buying [EdisonIndustrial — Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:00:41]; the Dolphin team hires local land-use counsel on every acquisition [CREDA Global — cKtqug8KPPk @ 00:01:12].

sop_steps.title: Clear Environmental and Site Infrastructure
sop_steps.action: Order a Phase I, carry environmental insurance from day one, and hold back funds pending no-further-action letters.
sop_steps.detail: Horowitz treats Phase I as mandatory, carries environmental insurance from day one, flags PFAS as an emerging issue, and uses holdbacks pending NFA letters [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:26:50]; Solberg calls Phase I non-negotiable and checks pavement thickness, drainage, and current stormwater permits [MaxLife Commercial RE MLR — oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:04:00].

sop_steps.title: Measure Usable Acres and Required Improvements
sop_steps.action: Net out landscaping, retention, and setbacks, and confirm city-required paving, drainage, lighting, or building before closing.
sop_steps.detail: EdisonIndustrial notes that cities may require paving, drainage, lighting, or an industrial building, which must be confirmed in diligence before closing [EdisonIndustrial — Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:01:39]; Jonathan Gonzalez warns that two 5-acre sites a few miles apart can differ entirely on zoning, usable acreage, access, and paving [Capright — p8t7CLKouHw @ 00:00:43].

sop_steps.title: Structure the Price and Seller Terms
sop_steps.action: Model vacancy into the basis, buy at a discount to stabilized pricing, and negotiate a tenant-finding window with a guaranteed floor.
sop_steps.detail: Ned asks sellers for a 3 to 4 month window to find a tenant with a guaranteed floor price [Industrial Real Estate Show — LftC_mcL69E @ 00:22:41], and buys Atlanta at 8.5 percent against 7 percent stabilized trades after modeling 6 to 8 months of vacancy [Industrial Real Estate Show — LftC_mcL69E @ 00:14:54].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Demand is the sharpest split. CBRE's Will Pike says every major industrial allocator now runs an IOS strategy, and Leo Addimando of Alterra frames the sector as infrastructure real estate hiding in plain sight [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:20:25]. The Industrial Advisors panel pushes back hard: Matt McGregor sees more fluff and talk than actual action, and Kyle Back sums it up, saying demand has been overstated a little bit [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:03:18]. Kyle's read is size-specific. Yards of 1 to 3 acres lease, while 5 to 7 acre sites sit because institutions push rates that are hard to pencil for truck and equipment users [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:03:05]. Edison Basquez lands on the same small-yard side, putting the perfect site under 5 acres with most users needing 1 to 3 [-7jTPPttg2s @ 00:00:53]. Ned of 9606 Capital plays the other end of the size curve, buying buildings of 3,000 to 50,000 square feet on 3 to 25 acres and recently closing a 78-acre Atlanta yard with 39 usable acres [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:22:04]. The operator read: small infill yards carry the deepest renter pool, while anything above 5 acres needs a rent that pencils for the user or a patient vacancy budget.

How far along the trade sits depends on who is talking. Ned of 9606 Capital calls the sector about 85% fully institutionalized, yet still mom-and-pop the way self-storage once was, with 5 to 6 years of runway left [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:06:42]. Addimando counters that under 10% of a $200 to $500 billion universe is institutionally owned [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:15:15]. Meg Aubale argues operators are still early precisely because Aubale's deals run about $5 million each, too small for institutions and short on direct comps, which is how stabilized yields above 12% survive [-s1lJ8WxV9o @ 00:03:00]. Pricing method splits along the same line. Addimando values per usable acre, provided a functional building sits on the yard, and puts valuation spreads to traditional industrial at 25 to 50 basis points, narrowed from 150 [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:12:53]. Jonathan Gonzalez of Capright says calling two 5-acre sites a few miles apart equal because both traded at X dollars per acre misses most of the story, since one may carry environmental constraints, unusable acreage or outdoor-use restrictions [p8t7CLKouHw @ 00:01:06]. Ned prices that risk directly: stabilized assets trade at a 7% cap, and Ned buys at 8.5% after modeling 6 to 8 months of vacancy [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:14:54].

Lease term is the third fault line. Ryan Solberg treats short leases as a feature and a risk in the same sentence: 1-to-3-year terms mark rents to market fast, but many carry 30-day termination rights [oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:03:38]. The Industrial Advisors panel sees 1-to-3-year and month-to-month deals as normal, and Matt McGregor even rents per-trailer stalls at about $250 with a 10-stall minimum, while admitting that is hard to manage [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:05:23]. McGregor also notes that typical capex is 9 to 18 inches of crushed rock or paving with near-zero cost between tenants [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:01:35]. Addimando runs the opposite book, managing Alterra to a rolling 5-year WALT and refusing months-long pop-up leases [WL25Tl_e2Gs @ 00:23:58]. Steve Azar of Ambient compares the setup to manufactured housing 20 years ago, underwrites 15-year holds, and notes that long 10-to-15-year leases leave many rents sitting below market [znP8wX2_k2w @ 00:36:38]. The exit story also splits inside one panel. Bill Condon says developers ride a roughly 5-year lease and then build, while McGregor counters that most such sites never got developed because IOS income is so lucrative [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:04:02]. Pick the lane deliberately: short paper buys mark-to-market speed and turnover risk, long paper buys stickiness and below-market rent drag.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Zoning is where buyers have actually lost. Edison Basquez reports that investors have bought non-compliant sites because industrial zoning does not automatically allow outdoor storage, and tells buyers to verify with the city, then price what it takes to make a yard compliant before closing [Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:01:02]. Chase MacLeod calls not fully confirming the allowed uses in the zoning code one of the biggest mistakes in the sector, even while marketing a $9 million Inland Empire yard with multiple by-right uses [m96MC6Qe9oM @ 00:02:16]. Steve Azar adds the grandfathering trap: a legal non-conforming use can disappear when the tenant leaves, and Southern California towns are cracking down on non-conforming sites, so Ambient runs in-house land-use work that goes deeper than the zoning report [znP8wX2_k2w @ 00:12:40]. Justin Horowitz of Cooper Horowitz calls zoning super super important and warns that a seller's municipal ties can hide zoning limits, which is why the hire is zoning counsel rather than the seller's word [yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:15:16]. The economics check is blunt: a yard that cannot legally host the tenant pool has no rent roll, so every price conversation starts with whether outdoor storage is permitted by right, what the city will allow, and who confirmed it.

The second trap is buying gross acres and leasing net ones. Edison Basquez shows landscaping, retention and setbacks eating 0.5 acre of a 2-acre site, leaving 1.5 usable acres, and warns tenants may pay only on the usable area [Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:02:33]. Gravel alone fails in Basquez's market because municipal code requires paving, drainage, fencing and lighting before tenants can even pull business licenses [-7jTPPttg2s @ 00:01:37]. Kyle Back watches gravel yards, narrow sites and sites reached through residential roads sit, while paved, fenced, lit yards with an office pull United Rentals-type credit, and Matt McGregor adds that long, narrow strips that cannot fit a truck court stay vacant [gvn8kH2TUE0 @ 00:06:45]. Ned budgets the fix in real dollars: light site work runs $75,000 to $125,000 per acre and heavy work $175,000 to $300,000, with Jacksonville near $225,000 and Chicago near $125,000 [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:29:59]. Ned cuts material cost by taking asphalt millings at $30 per truck versus a $50 dump fee, against $800 for a truck of gravel, and pre-approves shop buildings instead of building them since a metal shop takes 4 to 5 months [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:27:08]. Run the net usable acre count and the site-work budget before the deposit goes hard.

The third trap is buying the last cycle's rent. Steve Sprenger, a former trucker turned Inland Empire broker, saw more than 25 million square feet offered for sublease [tn1QmPINHeE @ 00:19:17], overseas 3PLs proposing 10-year leases with a year of free rent and then walking away, legacy leases running 15 to 20% above market, and land values down at least 50% [tn1QmPINHeE @ 00:21:39]. Ned watched LA and Inland Empire yard rents fall from $35,000 to $15,000-$18,000 [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:31:58], and called broker claims of $8,000 to $10,000 per acre per month in Atlanta mispricing when real rent sits near $5,000 [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:13:46]. The credit side bites too: Commercial Real Estate Now flags IOS tenants as local and regional operators with weak credit, some prone to bankruptcy, and says a buyer at a compressed cap rate planning a 3-year exit is a weaker fit, even though competing operators absorbing failed sites keeps credit losses low [dKQj8cpiqeE @ 00:03:03]. Andrew Smith of Carter Jonas calls the sector simple but hard and has watched £100 million leveraged portfolio plans struggle [4dMhVDuB-hM @ 00:45:53]. Ned's counterweight is balance-sheet discipline, running leverage under 35% across everything owned and carrying a 2.6 DSCR against the banks' 1.25 requirement [LftC_mcL69E @ 00:24:12]. Stress the rent to today's comps, not the last-cycle peak.

callout.title: Four Kill-Switches Before the Deposit Goes Hard
callout.body: Each item below is a pitfall practitioners watched cripple IOS deals. Clear all four before the deposit goes hard.
items: Confirm outdoor storage is allowed by right, not conditional, and that it is not a grandfathered legal non-conforming use that disappears when the tenant leaves [MaxLife Commercial RE MLR — oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:04:00].

Hire local land use counsel on every acquisition and meet the municipality on allowed activities and future tenant types, because the top three challenges are zoning, zoning, and zoning [CREDA Global — cKtqug8KPPk @ 00:01:12].
Measure usable acres net of landscaping, retention and setbacks, since a 2-acre site can lease as 1.5 acres and tenants may pay only on usable area [EdisonIndustrial — Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:02:48].

Order a Phase I, bind environmental insurance from day one, and negotiate holdbacks pending no-further-action letters, with PFAS flagged as an emerging issue [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:26:50].

chapters.pull_quote: "In IOS, the zoning and the dirt are the deal." — Ryan Solberg, MaxLife Commercial RE MLR (oYtLEutv1NQ @ 00:05:41).
action_checklist: Run the diligence sequence in order: confirm zoning, then environmental, then the leasing market, before calling a site gold [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:03:41].
Tour every site in person and test whether a 53-foot trailer can actually turn in before underwriting rent [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:06:44].
Pull comps from IOS List, appraisers and local brokers, kept within a 10-15 mile radius of the subject yard [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:34:18].
Ask the seller for a 3-4 month window to find a tenant with a guaranteed floor price, and model 6-8 months of vacancy into the bid [Industrial Real Estate Show — LftC_mcL69E @ 00:22:41].

Confirm city-required paving, drainage, lighting or an industrial building during diligence and before closing, then budget $75-125K per acre for light work or $175-300K for heavy work [EdisonIndustrial — Wu_IobArlaI @ 00:01:55].
Size debt to a 10% debt yield and 1.25x DSCR, and expect managed truck parking to need a 12-13% debt yield [Industrial Real Estate Show — yb3YiKWxoFg @ 00:21:12].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I develop and operate an IOS or truck parking yard, and what does it actually cost to make it work?
chapters.title: Building and Running IOS and Truck Parking Yards
chapters.subtitle: Raw land to IOS in San Antonio, actual truck parking development costs, zoning hurdles, flex vs. IOS, contractor yards (Longyards), managed truck parking challenges, gate and access control systems, and Rig Hut yard-management lessons
chapters.executive_summary: Operators building IOS and truck parking yards agree on a land-first, low-coverage thesis: zoning that allows outdoor storage by right, sites under roughly 20-30% building coverage, infill highway access, and a city that will actually sign off. Ron Rohde pushed DFW stall rents from $100 to $215-225 on a 5.5-acre yard, and models one acre at about 40 spaces at $175 per month. Build costs run $16 per linear foot for chain link, about $30K for a cantilever gate, and $1,000 per light pole, with self-management via Easy Storage, PDK text-to-gate, or Rig Hut app access tied to payment. Practitioners split on pavement versus gravel, single versus multi-tenant, padlocks versus automation, and daily versus monthly parkers, while Truck Parking Club runs a 70/30 marketplace split for hosts monetizing spare spaces.

key_metrics.label: Truck Stall Rent Lift
key_metrics.value: $100 to $215-225 per stall per month
key_metrics.context: Rohde's pro forma assumed a 50% bump to $150 per 75 ft x 12 ft stall on a 5.5-acre graveled yard; actual rents reached $215-225, but higher insurance kept net income flat.

key_metrics.label: One-Acre Truck Parking Gross and NOI
key_metrics.metric: One-Acre Truck Parking Gross and NOI
key_metrics.value: About 40 spaces x $175/mo = $7,000/mo gross; about $57K NOI
key_metrics.context: Unit math run on the Tyler Cauble show with occupancy in the mid-to-upper 90s, after taxes, insurance, management, utilities, and software; the hosts labeled it a 19% cap with no capex.

key_metrics.label: Marketplace Host Revenue Split
key_metrics.value: 70/30 owner/platform starting rate
key_metrics.context: Evan Shelley's Truck Parking Club split covers marketing, notifications, payment processing, 24/7/365 support, and payouts, with lower rates for operators running 5-10 lots.

key_metrics.label: Automatic Cantilever Gate Cost
key_metrics.value: About $30K installed for a 30 ft cantilever; operator about $5K
key_metrics.context: Rohde recommends an automatic gate even on Class B yards because manual gates get left open; the cantilever needs a 30-40% counterbalance, so the gate runs about 70 ft long.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator in this lane starts from the same rule Ron Rohde repeats: land first, buildings second. Rohde frames IOS as low-coverage yards for trucks, trailers, and equipment, with no roofs or major plumbing to fail and no $50K air-conditioning surprises [-g_D6hbOPNE @ 00:00:16]. Rohde tightens the definition to 20% or less site coverage by improvements, with zoning that allows outdoor storage by right, and warns that flood zones and geotech problems shrink what you can actually use [q7HQGiIiT_8 @ 00:02:49]. Benji Miller of Negresco Property Group lands in the same place from the SoCal institutional side: the ideal sites run 30% coverage or less with by-right zoning, and once a site crosses that line rent tips to a per-building basis, so 32.5% coverage with demolishable sheds is a different game [7qT_5Pw0cTo @ 00:28:35]. When a Chicago residential investor tried to define IOS by acreage and infill location, Rohde pushed back, arguing size and infill do not belong in the definition and it falls apart once building coverage passes 20-30% [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:02:19]. The operator takeaway: underwrite the dirt and the zoning entitlement first, treat any building as a leasing accelerator, and walk from sites where coverage pushes you into a different asset class.

The demand side is the one point nobody argues. Rohde pegs the gap at roughly 3 million tractor-trailers chasing about 300,000 paid commercial spaces while city regulation keeps eliminating truck parking, and says a single site can earn $10-30K per month [rPXHwXgqWs8 @ 00:00:37]. On Jonathan Hayek's show Rohde flagged the truck count as possibly misquoted but held the thesis: San Antonio fines trucks parked more than two consecutive days, one fine equals a month of parking, and the trucks being protected cost $75-100K apiece [mPrS0VognEo @ 00:29:24]. The binding constraint is entitled land, not tenants. The Truck N’ Hustle operator calls finding land zoned for truck parking the toughest part of the business and picked industrial zoning ringed by trash and window-manufacturing neighbors who won't complain [uZVNo7EIaXA @ 00:00:03]. Rohde hit the same wall on a 5.5-acre yard: the city was the number-one issue across zoning, setbacks, fire lanes, sprinklers, sewer, and utilities, and 50-75+ tours from national and credit groups produced no lease without the city's green light [gcg4K6xqYaU @ 00:05:42]. The consensus rule: confirm the jurisdiction is friendly before going under contract, never after, because Rohde was still on regulatory work 24 months after closing.

The baseline physical product is also settled: a secured, lit, fenced yard. Rohde's Class B standard is gravel, full fencing, a gate, and lighting with no frills, and the case for it is recession resilience, since $400 paved-lot parkers trade down in a downturn [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:19:05]. The Massachusetts Truck N’ Hustle operator's build list ran new pavement, striping with assigned numbered spots, about 33 perimeter light poles they called a huge expense, and CCTV with posted signs that is actually monitored [uZVNo7EIaXA @ 00:01:43]. Management is the other baseline. Rohde says IOS rents will not justify paying a third-party manager a few hundred to $1,000 a month, so owners self-manage, while multi-tenant flex can carry a property manager [-g_D6hbOPNE @ 00:04:39]. The Rig Hut founders, who handled roughly 1,000 vehicles a month around a South Florida port city, add that monthly tenants paying $250-400 are the business: daily parking pays more but carries the highest management intensity and the most gate and damage incidents, so learn monthly tenants' names, equipment, and anniversary billing dates [ulBXkeE5I_8 @ 00:03:11]. Those four pillars, entitled dirt, perimeter security, self-management, and a monthly core, are the floor every speaker builds on.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Sourcing starts off-market because brokers ignore the deal size. Rohde says DFW infill runs $300-500K an acre, too small for brokers to give the time of day, so the team built a list of 200-300 sites from Google Maps and PropStream, scored each on highway proximity, lot shape, slope, zoning, and owner or use, then hit the top 30-50 with texts, calls, flyers, and emails; host Tyler Cauble's own cadence is 600 properties a quarter, 10 a day, where a 1% response is good [q7HQGiIiT_8 @ 00:05:05]. The unit math is a 75-foot by 11-13-foot stall, about 900 square feet, which works out to 20-25 spaces per acre at roughly 50% coverage [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:31:22]. On the Cauble show the model ran about 40 spaces per acre at $175 a month for $7,000 gross, then taxes near $6K, insurance $2K, management $12K, utilities $6K, and software $1K, leaving about $57K of NOI the hosts labeled a 19% cap with no capex [q7HQGiIiT_8 @ 00:22:20]. To set the rent, Rohde tells operators to pull the Google Maps median, underwrite at or slightly below it, and validate with a $30-50 Facebook ad before committing [mPrS0VognEo @ 00:50:21].

Rohde's line-item truck parking budget is the closest thing to a price sheet in this niche. Land at $50-100K an acre can cash flow while $1M an acre likely won't; clearing runs $1-4K an acre plus dumpsters, grading about $5K an acre in infill DFW off a topographic survey pulled during diligence, and gravel is the single most expensive item [rPXHwXgqWs8 @ 00:01:28]. Fencing is $16 per linear foot for 6-foot chain link with top and bottom rails and three strands of barbed wire, measured off Google Maps or a boundary or ALTA survey, and the price doubles for R panel where a city bans chain link and demands opaque fencing [rPXHwXgqWs8 @ 00:05:27]. Rohde specs an automatic gate even at Class B because manual gates get left open: about $5K for a LiftMaster operator, about $30K installed for a 30-foot cantilever, and since a cantilever needs a 30-40% counterbalance the gate runs roughly 70 feet long, while rolling gates need concrete or asphalt because rocks derail them [rPXHwXgqWs8 @ 00:06:59]. Chris Long of Longyards, building modular fencing that slides into concrete, reported Florida fence quotes at $55 a foot and 3-8 acre build-outs at $300-800K [7n_O1KWl4EQ @ 00:35:36].

The operating stack is software plus remote access. Chris Long runs QR onboarding, Easy Storage Solutions with PDK text-to-gate, grid-labeled piles like B7, and view-only main-camera access for tenants with no audio and a posted disclosure, a setup Rohde said he plans to adopt [7n_O1KWl4EQ @ 00:24:21]. Jose of Rig Hut lays out the access ladder: padlock and chain needs on-site staff, a keypad gate operator assigns and expires codes per tenant or reservation as a strong middle ground, LPR logs in and out timestamps for high-value yards but demands connectivity, quality cameras, and subscriptions, and a mobile-app link opens the gate with no hardware [GOXjR9kZ3BA @ 00:01:54]. One Rig Hut client went from Zelle, Venmo, checks, cash, and inventory on a sheet of printer paper to phone-opened gates with timestamps, and locks out past-due tenants on the 10th, which generates calls [hjC6tiI5Kd4 @ 00:00:48]. Rohde sizes the labor: a minimum viable yard is about 4 acres grossing $7-8K a month, run by an offshore VA under $2K a month, and the VA tipping point sits at $8-10K gross, after which one VA lets you triple in size [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:27:03].

callout.title: Small Edges Yard Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Four moves practitioners use to squeeze more revenue and fewer headaches out of the same dirt.
items: Answer first or lose the truck: inbound callers are dialing three yards at once, and a 20-minute callback lost bookings, so get the caller into the system immediately [Truck Parking Media — ulBXkeE5I_8 @ 00:02:30]

Mark up vendor services on Class A yards: Rohde charges $225 for wash services the vendor prices at $200, alongside showers and a 24-hour golf-cart patrol at about $5K a month [Ronald Rohde Law — tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:14:14]

Skip commercial Wi-Fi: carriers see the address and quote a $150 monthly commercial minimum while SIM cards run about $10 each, and never mix the two technologies across one site [Ronald Rohde Law — tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:21:27]

Work the underutilized-yard play: spot candidates on Google Earth, count dock trailers as a utilization proxy, have the tenant give back 1.5 acres to save $3,000 a month, and re-lease at $6,000 NNN to turn a 6.25 cap into an 8 [Jonathan Hayek — mPrS0VognEo @ 00:22:53]

sop_steps.action: Confirm zoning, approvals, and environmental condition before going hard.

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fight is over what an IOS site even is, and the definition dictates what you buy. Ron Rohde, sitting with Tyler Cauble, draws the line at 20% or less site coverage by improvements, with outdoor storage allowed by right [q7HQGiIiT_8 @ 00:02:49]. Benji Miller of Negresco Property Group runs a looser box: 30% coverage or less with by-right zoning is ideal, and past that the rent tips toward a per-building basis, with 32.5% coverage and demolishable sheds being a different game [7qT_5Pw0cTo @ 00:28:35]. When a Chicago residential investor pitched IOS as 3 to 10 acre urban parcels near highways with outdoor-storage zoning, Ron pushed back, saying size and infill don't belong in the definition and that it falls apart above 20 to 30% building coverage [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:02:19]. The sharper split is building versus bare dirt. Ron told Jonathan Hayek flatly that a pure yard is off the menu in 2024, because a site without a building gets fewer accessory uses by right [mPrS0VognEo @ 00:08:57]. Benji lands in the same place from the leasing side: bare paved yards only make sense for drayage or trucking near the port, and sites with buildings lease better. The pure-yard operator lives or dies on port-adjacent drayage demand.

Surface and gate spend split the operators into two camps. The Truck N’ Hustle operator, running roughly 100 spots in Massachusetts at about $500 per spot per month, puts pavement at the top of the build list: number one is you want pavement, not crush gravel, followed by striping, numbered spots, around 33 perimeter light poles and CCTV that is actually monitored [uZVNo7EIaXA @ 00:01:43]. Ron Rohde runs the opposite playbook in DFW. Ron's pick is Class B: gravel, full fencing, a gate and lighting with no frills, which Ron calls recession-resilient because $400 paved-lot parkers trade down when the market tightens [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:19:05]. On gates, Ron still tells builders to install an automatic gate even at Class B, because manual gates get left open, and prices a 30 ft cantilever gate with install at about $30K [rPXHwXgqWs8 @ 00:06:59]. Jose at Rig Hut takes the staged route: test the market under a lease with manual gates before investing in automation, then move to an automatic system once you want 24/7 access, multiple tenants and expansion beyond one location [Fc82YDH9IrI @ 00:06:10]. Jose concedes that five-acre gravel lots in tight markets get away with padlocks purely because demand is high.

Tenant concentration and rental term are the third fault line. Ron Rohde argues single tenant is a benefit: underwrite heavily and bet once, because in a building of 20 to 30 flex tenants at least 5 are financially shaky [-g_D6hbOPNE @ 00:02:17]. Ron frames the choice as a temperament call: with sweat equity, choose multi-tenant; if time-constrained, choose single tenant. The Truck N’ Hustle operator leans on the opposite logic and treats many tenants as a shield: with 50 tenants, losing 2 doesn't hurt, though they concede a single tenant is simpler to run and eventually leased the first lot to one tenant [uZVNo7EIaXA @ 00:04:16]. On term, Ron's math favors transient parking: $30 a night is about $900 a month per space against $225 to $300 from a monthly tenant, and even at 80% occupancy a daily space yields about $630, but it demands heavy marketing through Facebook, trucker apps, forums and signage [tonuCLfZrYE @ 00:10:32]. Rig Hut, having handled about 1,000 vehicles a month at peak around a South Florida port city, lands on the other side: daily and transient pays more but brings the highest management intensity and more gate and damage incidents, so monthly tenants paying $250 to $400 are the business [ulBXkeE5I_8 @ 00:02:56].
